phase1_inventory.scientific_basis: The Bessis Hamiltonian H = p^2 + x^2 + i x^3 is claimed, on numerical evidence, to have an entirely real and positive spectrum; its eigenvalues can be computed independently and checked for reality and positivity.

The paper contrasts H = p^2 + i x^3 + i x, whose entire spectrum is claimed positive, with H = p^2 + i x^3 + x, whose entire spectrum is claimed complex; both spectral assertions are numerically falsifiable.
For H = p^2 + x^2 the exact oscillator spectrum is E_n = 2n + 1, providing a reproducible analytic and numerical baseline.
For H = p^2 + x^2 + i x the paper gives the exact positive spectrum E_n = 2n + 5/4, which can be checked by a complex coordinate shift or direct diagonalization.
For H = p^2 + x^2 - x, with parity defined about x = 1/2, the paper gives E_n = 2n + 3/4; the constant spectral shift is exactly testable.
For H = p^2 + x^2 + i x - x the paper gives the complex spectrum E_n = 2n + 1 + i/2; its real and imaginary parts are exactly testable.

The plotted massless eigenvalue branches of H = p^2 - (i x)^N versus N encode many numerical energies, level-merger locations, the three spectral regimes, the N <= 1.42207 last-real-level threshold, and divergences near N = 1 and at large N.

phase1_inventory.scientific_basis: For m = 0 and N >= 2 the spectrum is claimed infinite, discrete, entirely real and positive, with N = 2 reducing to E_n = 2n + 1 and N = 4 giving the positive discrete spectrum of p^2 - x^4; these statements can be tested across N and level index.

phase1_inventory.scientific_basis: For 1 < N < 2 only finitely many eigenvalues remain real and positive while higher adjacent levels merge into complex-conjugate pairs; at N <= 1.42207 only the ground-state eigenvalue remains real.

phase1_inventory.source_ref: p. 2, first column; p. 3, discussion after Eq. (3)
phase1_inventory.scientific_basis: At N = 1 the contour problem has no eigenvalue, for N <= 1 there are no real eigenvalues, and the ground-state energy diverges as N approaches 1 from above; direct spectral computations and the Airy limit can falsify this boundary claim.
Fig. 2 is a schematic of the complex-x contour, Stokes wedges, cut, and axes for N = 4.2; it contains no plotted numerical dataset or independent subpanel.

The left and right anti-Stokes angles are specified by Eq. (3), the wedge opening is Delta = 2 pi/(N + 2), the wedges contain the real axis for 1 < N < 4, and at N = 1 their opening and centers are 2 pi/3, 5 pi/6, and pi/6; all follow from quantitative asymptotics.

The eigenvalue problem is claimed invariant under deformation to any integration contour whose two ends approach infinity inside the selected left and right wedges; numerical spectra obtained on distinct admissible contours can test this claim.

The selected turning points x_- and x_+ are given explicitly as functions of E and N and are claimed to lie in the lower half-plane for N > 2 and upper half-plane for N < 2; substitution and branch tracking provide direct checks.

phase1_inventory.scientific_basis: Eigenvalues used in Fig. 1 are claimed to agree between a coupled-real-equation Runge-Kutta shooting/patching method and an independent truncated harmonic-oscillator matrix diagonalization; this is a reproducible two-solver cross-check.

phase1_inventory.source_ref: p. 3, WKB phase-integral paragraph before Eq. (5)
phase1_inventory.scientific_basis: The leading WKB turning-point path is continuous and real-valued for N >= 2 but crosses the positive-imaginary-axis branch cut and fails to join the turning points continuously for N < 2; contour evaluation can falsify this domain-of-validity claim.

phase1_inventory.source_ref: Eq. (5) and surrounding semiclassical discussion, p. 3
phase1_inventory.scientific_basis: For N >= 2 the paper gives an explicit leading-order WKB asymptotic formula for E_n as n tends to infinity, including its Gamma-function, sin(pi/N), and exponent dependence; exact numerical spectra can test its values and convergence.
Table I reports exact Runge-Kutta and WKB eigenvalues for n = 0,...,4 at N = 3 and n = 0,...,3 at N = 4; all 18 printed values and their pairwise discrepancies are directly reproducible.

For the |x|^N potential, leading WKB is claimed to omit sin(pi/N), remain valid for N > 0, and approach square-well energies (n + 1)^2 pi^2/4 as N tends to infinity, while the -(i x)^N energies diverge.

At N = 1 the decaying Airy solutions on the 30-degree and 150-degree rays give a patching derivative equal to -1/(2 pi), not zero, so no real eigenvalue exists; the identity and conclusion can be checked analytically and numerically.

For N = 1 + epsilon the ground-state energy is governed by the printed implicit asymptotic equation and roughly scales as E proportional to (-ln epsilon)^(2/3); numerical root solutions and direct eigenvalues can test the asymptotic claim.
Table II gives exact and Eq. (11) asymptotic ground-state energies at seven epsilon = N - 1 values from 10^-1 through 10^-7; all 21 printed entries and the trend of the error are reproducible.

For N = 2 - epsilon the expansion (i x)^(2-epsilon) is claimed to yield a non-Hermitian logarithmic perturbation that makes adjacent harmonic-oscillator levels merge rather than repel as epsilon tends to zero from above.

phase1_inventory.source_ref: Eq. (12) and preceding classical discussion, p. 4
phase1_inventory.scientific_basis: For m = 0 and N >= 2 the complex classical trajectory joining the selected turning points is periodic with the explicit real period T in Eq. (12); quadrature or trajectory integration can test the formula.

For N < 2 the classical path misses the partner turning point, spirals across Riemann sheets toward a stated asymptotic angle, has infinite period, and acquires additional encountered turning points in one-to-one correspondence with quantum level mergers as N approaches 2 from below.

For m nonzero the paper claims transitions at N = 2 and N = 1: levels reemerge in pairs as N approaches 1 from above, the spectrum is entirely real and positive at N = 1, levels disappear again below N = 1 including the ground state, and an infinite real spectrum reappears as N tends to zero.

Fig. 3 plots massive-case eigenvalue branches versus N for m^2 = 3/16, 5/16, and 7/16 and displays the N = 2 and N = 1 transition structure; the individual branch values and mergers are numerical targets.
